focus_writing_final.title: Can Bangladesh Escape the Low-Growth Trap?
thesis: Economic growth signals higher production, income, investment and jobs.
Sustainable recovery needs investment, sound banks, stable prices and employment
glance: Economic problem Low-Growth Trap

Newly poor, source estimate 'About 2.1 million in FY2025-26

sections: Key points
Slower expansion
Weak manufacturing, exports and private investment are constraining growth
High inflation
Rising prices for necessities reduce real earnings and purchasing power, weakening domestic consumption
Stagnant private investment
High interest rates, uncertain energy supply and inconsistent policy discourage new factories and hiring
Poverty and labour-market stress
A World Bank assessment cited for October 2026 estimates around 2.1 million additional people entered poverty in FY2025-26
Importance and Opportunities
Banking weaknesses
Nonperforming loans, poor governance and irregular lending restrict credit to productive firms
Energy and infrastructure
Unreliable power and gas increase manufacturing costs and reduce competitiveness
Weak revenue collection
Insufficient taxation and other public revenues limit spending on health, education, infrastructure and safety nets
External uncertainty
Conflict, energy-price increases and unstable global trade raise import and production costs.
Major Challenges
Fewer jobs
Weak investment reduces employment opportunities in industry and services, especially for educated young people.
Higher poverty and inequality
Inflation raises living costs while wage and employment opportunities remain limited
Fiscal constraints
Slow output and poor revenue restrict Inclusive Recovery development spending and make debt-servicing obligations harder to manage
Reduced investor confidence
Policy and macroeconomic uncertainty discourage investment, exports and technological upgrading.
end: Bangladesh can avoid a prolonged growth trap if it restores confidence in banks and public institutions, stabilises prices and supports productive investment.

Those political outcomes may increase pressure for accountability but do not automatically end the war

Israeli coalition uncertainty

US congressional change

Public concern about war
Military costs and rising living expenses may strengthen anti-war opinion among voters
Changes in political checks
Coalition formation in Israel and opposition oversight in Washington may complicate decisions about continuing military operations

Congressional accountability
US legislators can hold hearings, investigate executive war policy and review budgets
Coalition dependence in Israel
Without a parliamentary majority, Netanyahu would require other parties' backing to form or sustain a government

thesis: Trade partnerships contribute to industrial development, investment and jobs.
These developments create opportunities rather than guaranteed commercial outcomes

Expanding initiatives
Business representatives discussed broader trade and investment during November 2026 and signed a cooperation memorandum

Importance and Opportunities
Export diversification
Garments, pharmaceuticals, jute, leather and processed food could reach more customers in Russia
Energy security
Cooperation in oil, gas and power may diversify Bangladesh's energy sources and support industrial output
Agriculture and food security
Russian wheat and fertiliser are important imports, with scope for collaboration in modern farming technology
Joint investment and skills
Practical partnerships in industry, science and ICT can enable technology transfer and employment.

Sanctions compliance
International restrictions affecting Russia complicate banking and regulatory assessments even for otherwise lawful trade.

Regional trade

english_focus.title: LDC Graduation: Reasons for Delay and Role of Trade Diplomacy
parts: Introduction
Bangladesh met all LDC graduation criteria in 2018 and 2021 and was due to graduate on 24 November 2026.
Due to practical realities and a lack of preparation for post-graduation challenges, the timeline was extended by 3 years to 2029.
Challenges (Reasons for Delay)

Global economic slowdown: recession and market instability hurt domestic industries.
Weak domestic industries: lack capacity to compete without preferences.
Preparation gap: long-term deficit in concluding essential trade agreements.
Post-graduation risks: loss of duty-free access, RMG tariff exposure, loss of WTO flexibilities (subsidies, patents)
Opportunities (Role of Trade Diplomacy)

Alternative markets: FTAs/PTAs with the EU, China, India, Japan.
Lower RMG tariff burden through specific lobbying.
EU GSP+: tariff-free entry, but requires meeting 27 international conventions.
Extended WTO transition on patents and subsidies beyond 2029.
Pharma protection: TRIPS waiver even after graduation.
Regional blocs such as RCEP
Policy Recommendations

Prioritise FTAs/PTAs with the EU, UK, Japan, China, India, ASEAN.
Implement the 27 GSP+ conventions (labour rights, environment).
Diversify exports: leather, pharma, ICT, agro-processing, light engineering.
Build a skilled trade-negotiation cadre and think tank.
Cut cost of doing business, improve ports and logistics, raise tax-GDP ratio.
Support SMEs with skills, technology and quality.
Coordinate with BGMEA, DCCI and development partners
Conclusion
LDC graduation is a milestone, not the end of the road.
The extension to 2029 is a precious window to build competitiveness.

english_focus.title: Sustainable Transformation of the Rural Economy
parts: Introduction
The rural economy covers economic activity outside cities: the farm sector (crops, livestock, fisheries, forestry) and the non-farm sector (cottage industry, trade, services).
It is the base of the national economy
Challenges
Climate change and disasters, shrinking farmland, high input costs, exploitative middlemen, weak cold storage, inflation, the digital divide, and rural youth migration to cities
Opportunities
Agriculture gives about 11% of GDP and employs about 45% of workers.
The rural economy supports food security, remittance use, a large domestic market, women's empowerment and agro-processing exports
Policy Recommendations
Smart, climate-resilient agriculture; regional cold chains; digital supply chains; agro-processing zones; fair prices; rural IT and freelancing training; better rural infrastructure
Conclusion
A nation's development is sustainable only when prosperity reaches its villages

english_focus.title: Trade Liberalization: Opportunities and Vulnerabilities
parts: Introduction
Trade liberalization means removing or reducing barriers such as tariffs and quotas.
For Bangladesh it is a double-edged sword, and after LDC graduation it is a necessity
Challenges
Sharp fall in government tariff revenue, threat of global giants crushing local SMEs, and rising import dependence
Opportunities
Export diversification beyond RMG, FTAs, and cheaper raw materials for local industry
Policy Recommendations
Phase tariff cuts gradually, protect infant industries, build alternative revenue sources, negotiate FTAs, and support SME competitiveness
Conclusion
Success needs a balanced approach that embraces global trade without leaving domestic industries unprotected

english_focus.title: Demographic Dividend and Human Resources Development
parts: Introduction
The demographic dividend is a window of opportunity that closes quickly.
About 65% of Bangladesh's population (about 11.9 crore) is of working age (15-64)
Challenges
Youth unemployment, skill mismatch, weak education quality, brain drain, low female labour participation, and an informal labour market
Opportunities
Large labour force, higher savings and investment, remittances, a bigger domestic market, and a chance to reach middle-income status
Policy Recommendations
Technical and vocational education, ICT and AI skills, manufacturing jobs, better health care, women's participation, and export of skilled labour
Conclusion
Turning population into human resources is the only way to convert the dividend into development

english_focus.title: Rural Economy: Sustainable Transformation for Inclusive Growth
parts: Introduction
The rural economy supports over 60% of the population and employs about 40% of the labour force.
It safeguards food security and channels remittances into the domestic market
Challenges
Climate-induced disasters, high production costs, exploitative middlemen, and rapid rural-to-urban youth migration
Opportunities
Climate-resilient agritech, rural agro-processing, digital supply chains, and freelancing for rural youth
Policy Recommendations
Modernize rural infrastructure, expand agro-processing, remove market inefficiencies through digital supply chains, and provide IT skills
Conclusion
A smart, sustainable rural transformation will build localized wealth and inclusive growth

english_focus.title: 3-R Strategy
parts: Introduction
The 3-R framework (Recovery, Restoration, Reconstruction) is the government's five-year plan (July 2026 - June 2031) for post-2024 state reform, economic recovery and democratic transition.
The PM presented it at the 81st UNGA
Challenges
Banking looting and the economic legacy of the previous regime, inflation, weak institutions, risk of authoritarian relapse, and fragile reserves
Opportunities
A reform mandate, international support, and a chance to modernize the economy and rebuild the state
Policy Recommendations

Recovery (1 year): stabilize macro indicators, control inflation, strengthen reserves, expand social safety nets.
Restoration (1-3 years): reform revenue system, banking, capital market and democratic institutions (police, EC, judiciary).
Reconstruction (next 5 years): tech-driven economy, human resources, digital transformation, long-term energy security
Conclusion
Disciplined sequencing of the three phases can turn crisis into a durable, democratic economic transformation

english_focus.title: Mecca Agreement and Bangladesh
parts: Introduction
Like NATO's Article 5, it treats an attack on one member as an attack on all
Challenges
Avoiding entanglement in military blocs, balancing relations with India and China, and risks to remittances and energy supplies from Middle East instability
Opportunities
Closer ties with the Muslim world, labour market and remittance security, and defence and energy cooperation
Policy Recommendations
Put national interest first, practise balanced and non-aligned diplomacy, decide only after parliamentary and expert review, and pursue economic rather than military gains
Conclusion
Bangladesh's priority should be maximum benefit through a strategic, balanced foreign policy, not mere participation

english_focus.title: Microplastics in the Food Chain
parts: Introduction
Microplastics are plastic fragments smaller than 5 mm.
They have entered rivers, the Bay of Bengal and our food, including hilsa, salt, sugar and soybean oil
Challenges
Uncontrolled plastic use and waste, weak waste management, and low awareness.
Particles can reach the lungs, liver, kidneys and stomach, and carry cancer risks from attached chemicals
Opportunities
Growing research, global attention to plastic treaties, and scope for a circular economy and alternatives such as jute
Policy Recommendations
Enforce the polythene ban, promote jute and biodegradable packaging, improve waste collection and recycling, monitor food safety, and run awareness campaigns
Conclusion
Protecting public health from this silent killer is a fight for survival, not just a slogan

english_focus.title: Semiconductor Industry
parts: Introduction
Semiconductors are at the center of global competition and drive AI, data centers, EVs and defence.
After RMG, the PM sees them as Bangladesh's next potential sector
Challenges
High capital and technology needs, scarce skilled engineers, unstable power, a weak R&D; base, and geopolitical competition
Opportunities
A young talent pool, chip design and back-end (assembly, testing) niches, supply-chain diversification, and FDI
Policy Recommendations
Prepare a national semiconductor policy, train engineers, create special economic zones with stable power, offer tax incentives, and partner with universities and global firms
Conclusion
With strategic policy and skilled youth, Bangladesh can enter the high-tech chip design market

english_focus.title: Democratic Movement and the Role of Youth
parts: Introduction
Youth is a spirit of revolt against injustice.
From the 1952 Language Movement to the 2024 mass uprising, youth have shed blood for democracy
Challenges
Politicization of students, unemployment, repression, weak institutions, and misinformation
Opportunities
Large youth energy, digital awareness, and the moral authority to build a non-discriminatory, free and equal state
Policy Recommendations
Ensure free campus politics, create jobs and skills, give youth a role in policy-making, and strengthen democratic institutions
Conclusion
Youth guard democracy and nation-building, provided their energy is channelled constructively

english_focus.title: Super El Nino and Bangladesh
parts: Introduction
The 2026 event is projected to be among the strongest in 150 years
Challenges
Crop failure (especially Aman), billions of dollars in losses, severe load-shedding, heatstroke and other health risks
Opportunities
Early warning systems, heat-tolerant crop varieties, and global climate finance
Policy Recommendations
Develop climate-resilient seeds, build food stocks, expand renewable energy, set up early warning and health preparedness, and strengthen climate diplomacy
Conclusion
El Nino is a climate alarm.
Early preparedness is critical for a vulnerable delta

english_focus.title: Creative Economy
parts: Introduction
The creative economy turns human creativity, culture and intellectual property into products, jobs and wealth.
UNESCO defines it as knowledge-based activity relying on individual creativity, skills and cultural assets
Challenges
Weak IP protection, scarce finance, limited skills and infrastructure, and lack of formal recognition
Opportunities
ICT and software, digital content, film and OTT, music, gaming and animation, fashion and textile design, EdTech, and a young connected population
Policy Recommendations
Enforce copyright, create creative-industry funds and incubators, provide training, and promote exports
Conclusion
The creative economy can diversify exports and build a knowledge-based economy

english_focus.title: Inclusive Development
parts: Introduction
Inclusive development ensures benefits are distributed equitably across all segments of society, 'leaving no one behind.'
Challenges
High inflation, weak private investment, unemployment, informal labour, climate risk, weak revenue collection, and rising inequality
Opportunities
Demographic dividend, remittances, export diversification, digital financial inclusion, women's employment, and safety nets such as the Family Card.
Aligns with SDGs 1, 4, 5, 8 and 10
Policy Recommendations
Control inflation, improve the investment climate, expand skills training, ensure banking governance, set minimum wages for informal workers, and raise revenue
Conclusion
Growth must be made inclusive for development to be sustainable

english_focus.title: Private Sector Credit Flow
parts: Introduction
Private sector credit is the loan banks give to businesses, industries and entrepreneurs.
It is a key indicator of investment and job creation
Challenges
Growth fell to a record low of about 4.7% in FY2025-26 (from about 13% in FY2021-22).
Causes: government borrowing from banks, high interest rates, liquidity crisis, high defaulted loans, and gas and power shortages
Opportunities
Reform can revive investment, productive manufacturing, SMEs and job creation
Policy Recommendations

Reduce government bank borrowing, raise revenue, stabilize interest rates, create special funds for productive sectors, ensure collateral-free SME and agri credit, restore trust in banks, and ensure gas and power supply
Conclusion
Revival of private credit is vital for growth and employment

english_focus.title: Digital Economy
parts: Introduction
The digital economy is economic activity driven by the internet, digital technology and data
Challenges
Skill gaps, brain drain, the digital divide, slow and costly internet, cyber and data security risks, weak digital literacy, and low FDI
Opportunities
ICT export potential (about $5 billion), a large freelancer base, mobile financial services (bKash, Nagad), cashless payments, e-commerce, e-governance and online education
Policy Recommendations
Train youth in AI, data science and cloud computing, update curricula, expand affordable broadband, strengthen cybersecurity and data protection laws, and support startups
Conclusion
A secure, inclusive digital ecosystem can power Bangladesh's next growth leap

english_focus.title: Violence Against Women and Children
parts: Introduction
Bangladesh ranks 24th on the Global Gender Gap Index 2025, yet violence against women and children remains widespread
Challenges
A 27% rise in rape cases against a conviction rate of only about 3% (ASK), a slow justice system, social stigma, impunity, and weak law enforcement
Opportunities
Public mobilization, strong women's participation, and legal frameworks that can be enforced
Policy Recommendations
Fast-track tribunals, victim protection and support, police sensitivity, awareness campaigns, safe public transport and spaces, and stronger investigation and prosecution
Conclusion
Violence against women stunts economic growth, so safety must match the progress on paper

english_focus.title: Leather Industry of Bangladesh
parts: Introduction
The leather industry is the second largest forex earner after RMG.
It relies mostly on domestic raw materials and is called a 'sleeping giant.'
Challenges
Lack of modernization, environmental non-compliance (tannery waste), weak international certification, and limited value addition
Opportunities
Potential to earn over $5 billion annually, higher value-added goods, and premium export prices
Policy Recommendations

Fully operationalize the Savar tannery estate with an effective central ETP, ensure compliance and international certification, support modern technology, and diversify into finished leather goods and footwear
Conclusion
With environmental compliance, the sector can become a major export earner

english_focus.title: Climate Change: Impact on Bangladesh
parts: Introduction
Climate change is the long-term change in global weather patterns, mainly through human-driven global warming.
Bangladesh is among the most vulnerable countries despite contributing little to emissions
Challenges
Floods, cyclones, salinity, sea-level rise, crop damage, displacement, and economic losses
Opportunities
Climate finance, adaptation expertise, renewable energy, and green investment
Policy Recommendations
Climate-resilient agriculture and infrastructure, renewable energy expansion, reforestation, early warning systems, access to the Loss and Damage fund, and strong climate diplomacy
Conclusion
We are the first generation to feel climate change and the last that can act against it

english_focus.title: Social Safety Net Programs
parts: Introduction
Social safety nets provide financial and social support to the poor, vulnerable, elderly and disabled so they can maintain a minimum standard of living
Challenges
Inflation, energy shortages, rising inequality, leakage and exclusion errors, fragmented programs, and climate shocks
Opportunities
Reducing poverty and inequality, building human capital, boosting social cohesion, and digital delivery (Family Card, Krishak Card)
Policy Recommendations
Consolidate programs, use digital identification and payment, prevent leakage, increase allocations (FY27: Tk 1.44 lakh crore), and target the extreme poor
Conclusion
It is a tool for a discrimination-free, humane Bangladesh, not just aid for the poor

english_focus.title: Role of the CSME Sector
parts: Introduction
The CSME (cottage, small and medium enterprise) sector is the backbone of the economy.
It supplies about 85% of industrial employment and contributes about a quarter of GDP
Challenges
Limited access to finance, high interest rates, the dollar crisis, market competition, weak technology and skills, and licensing complexity
Opportunities
Job creation, rural development, import substitution and export diversification
Policy Recommendations
Collateral-free and low-interest credit, a CSME refinance fund, technology and skills support, simplified licensing, market linkage, and digital platforms
Conclusion
CSMEs are the frontline fighters against the current economic crisis and must be backed

english_focus.title: Bangladesh in the Nuclear Age (Rooppur)
parts: Introduction
Bangladesh became the 33rd nuclear country.
On 28 April 2026, fuel was loaded into Rooppur's first unit, marking the nuclear age
Challenges
Dependence on imported fuel and gas, high cost, nuclear safety and waste management, a skilled workforce, and grid integration
Opportunities
Stable, low-carbon baseload power, long-term energy security, and industrial and technological advancement
Policy Recommendations
Train nuclear professionals, strengthen the regulator and safety culture, upgrade the transmission grid, plan waste management, and diversify energy sources
Conclusion
Rooppur is a symbol of Bangladesh's self-respect and technological capability

english_focus.title: Role of Agriculture in the Economy
parts: Introduction
Agriculture drove Bangladesh's journey from 'bottomless basket' to a progressing economy.
Its GDP share is about 11% (FY25: 11.03%), but it remains vital
Challenges
Declining arable land, climate change, high input costs, middlemen, weak storage and low value addition
Opportunities
Food security, rural jobs, poverty reduction, inflation control, and agro-processing exports
Policy Recommendations
Mechanization, high-yield and climate-tolerant seeds, subsidies and fair prices, cold storage, agri-credit, and agro-processing
Conclusion
As Borlaug said, 'Everything else can wait, agriculture can't.'

english_focus.title: Gig Economy
parts: Introduction
The gig economy is a market of short-term, contract or freelance work, usually through digital platforms (Uber, Foodpanda)
Challenges
No job security, no social protection, unstable income, platform dependence and weak labour law coverage
Opportunities
Flexibility and independence, youth employment, freelancing (earning foreign currency), ride-sharing and e-commerce work
Policy Recommendations
Recognize gig workers legally, ensure minimum pay and insurance, provide skills training, and regulate platforms
Conclusion
Properly regulated, it can offer independence and income without exploiting workers

english_focus.title: Money Laundering in Bangladesh
parts: Introduction
Money laundering is a critical threat.
An estimated $12-15 billion a year was siphoned out over 15 years (TIB) through trade misinvoicing, corruption and hundi
Challenges
Crony capitalism, weak enforcement and political influence, poor bank governance, and difficulty recovering assets
Opportunities
Recovering stolen assets, international cooperation, and rebuilding trust in banks
Policy Recommendations
Strengthen BFIU and the ACC, tighten trade monitoring, ensure beneficial ownership transparency, cooperate internationally on asset recovery, and promote legal remittance over hundi
Conclusion
Stopping illicit outflow is essential to protect Bangladesh's economic gains

english_focus.title: Family Card
parts: Introduction
The Family Card is a new social safety net initiative based on the idea that the family, not the individual, is the unit of development
Challenges
Accurate beneficiary identification, digital infrastructure, leakage, funding, and coordination across agencies
Opportunities
Integrated cash, food, education and agri support through one card, with poverty reduction and women's empowerment.
Eligible Groups Landless and homeless families, families with a disabled member, elderly and minority groups, owners of 0.50 acre or less, and poor female-headed families
Policy Recommendations
Build a unified database, ensure transparency and digital payments, monitor regularly, and phase in rollout
Conclusion
It moves Bangladesh toward a welfare state

english_focus.title: Liquidity Crisis
parts: Introduction
Banks' liquidity crisis in 2025 is complex and critical.
Central bank emergency support has kept the system running, but good governance is needed to restore stability
Challenges (Causes)
High defaulted loans, weak governance and political influence, forex crisis, loss of public trust, money laundering, slow recovery, and capital shortfall
Opportunities
Reform momentum: Bank Resolution Ordinance 2025, mergers of weak banks, higher deposit insurance (Tk 2 lakh), IFRS-9, Basel III and risk-based supervision
Policy Recommendations
Special tribunals for defaulters, stop rescheduling facilities, set up an asset management company (AMC), ensure central bank independence, enforce accountability, and bring back laundered money
Conclusion
Good governance is the key to restoring liquidity and trust

english_focus.title: Defaulted (Willful/Bad) Loans
parts: Introduction
More than one-third of bank loans are now defaulted, about Tk 6 lakh crore.
A third of lent money is stuck
Challenges (Causes and Impacts)
Causes: political interference, weak governance, wilful default, repeated rescheduling, weak legal enforcement, slow courts.
Impacts: liquidity crisis, loss of trust, reduced investment and growth, high interest rates, risk of bank failure
Opportunities
Reform and recovery can restore bank health, free up credit and revive investment
Policy Recommendations
Special tribunals and speedy case resolution, strict enforcement, asset recovery, an AMC, central bank autonomy, and independent supervision
Conclusion
Defaulted loans are the 'bleeding' of the economy.
Sustainable development is impossible unless it stops

english_focus.title: 4IR and the Banking Sector
parts: Introduction
The Fourth Industrial Revolution, driven by AI, Big Data, blockchain and IoT, is reshaping banking from physical operations to data-driven, digital, personalized services
Challenges
Cybersecurity and fraud risk, high technology cost, skill gaps, legacy systems, weak regulation, and job displacement
Opportunities
Efficiency, security, better customer experience, AI-based credit scoring, fraud detection, new business models and financial inclusion
Policy Recommendations
Invest in technology and cybersecurity, train bankers, update regulation, adopt fintech and open banking, and expand digital infrastructure
Conclusion
Banks that embrace 4IR will lead; those that don't will be left behind
